explain.say: Have you ever wondered how the coins in your pocket are made? Millions are made every day in factories called mints. Look at the first stage. It starts with huge rolls of metal, squeezed between rollers to exactly the thickness of a coin.

explain.say: See the scissors? A giant press punches round discs out of the strip, like a cookie cutter, hundreds at a time. These plain discs are called blanks. What do you think happens to the leftover metal full of holes?

explain.say: It's melted and reused! Look at the fire. The blanks are heated to soften them, then washed and polished until they shine. Next, at the wheel, a machine squeezes each edge to raise a little rim, which protects the picture from wearing away.

explain.say: Here's the big moment, see the piston? Each blank sits between two hard steel stamps called dies, with the pictures carved backwards. The press slams down with huge force and stamps both sides at once. Some presses strike hundreds of coins a minute! What pictures are on a coin you own?

explain.say: Finally, coins are checked, counted, bagged and sent to banks. Well done! Wow: the scientist Isaac Newton ran Britain's Royal Mint for about 30 years and chased down coin forgers! Challenge: look closely at a coin's edge. Is it smooth, ridged, or does it have writing?

faq.a: A plain metal disc punched out of a metal strip, before any pictures are stamped on it. Blanks are also called planchets.

faq.q: How are pictures stamped onto coins?
faq.a: A coin press squeezes the blank between two steel dies carved with the designs in reverse. One mighty strike stamps both sides at once.

faq.q: Why do coins have a raised rim?
faq.a: The rim protects the design from rubbing away and helps coins stack neatly.
asks: What is the rim of a coin for?

faq.q: Why do some coins have ridged edges?
faq.a: Long ago, coins were made of silver and gold, and people shaved metal off the edges. Ridges made shaving easy to spot. Today, different edges also help people, including blind people, tell coins apart by touch.

faq.q: Who decides what goes on a coin?
faq.a: Each country's government or central bank chooses the designs, often national symbols, famous people, animals or plants.

facts: Coin presses strike both sides of a coin at once using two dies.
Isaac Newton served at the Royal Mint, as Warden and then Master, from 1696 until his death in 1727.
